q: What does GAAP stand for?
r: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles
It is the common set of rules for financial reporting.
w: This is not the name of the standards.
GAAP is not set by one government approval.

q: Which organization sets GAAP for businesses in the United States?
r: The Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB)
FASB writes the accounting standards.
w: The Federal Reserve oversees monetary policy.

q: Which agency requires public companies to file financial reports with it?
r: The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)
It protects investors in public markets.
w: It handles competition and consumer protection.
The Occupational Safety and Health Administration

q: What is an audit?
r: An independent examination of financial records and statements
Auditors give an opinion on whether statements are fairly presented.
w: A tax payment made each quarter
That is an estimated tax payment.

q: What is an internal control?
r: A policy or procedure that protects assets and keeps records accurate
Examples include approvals and separation of duties.
w: A rule that sets the company's prices
Internal controls are set by the business.

q: What is fraud?
r: Intentional deception for personal gain
It involves a deliberate act.
w: An honest mistake in a calculation
A late payment to a vendor
This is a delay, not deception.

q: Which is an example of separation of duties?
r: One person records sales and another handles the cash
No one person controls a transaction from start to finish.
w: One person opens the mail, records and deposits cash
One person has too much control.
The owner signs checks alone with no review

q: Why should checks be prenumbered?
r: So missing or unauthorized checks can be detected
A gap in the sequence signals a problem.
w: To make checks harder to cash

q: Why should cash receipts be deposited daily?
r: To reduce the risk of loss or theft
Cash held on site is vulnerable.

q: What does the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX) mainly aim to do?
r: Improve the accuracy of public company financial reporting
It was passed after major accounting scandals.
w: Wages are set by other laws.

q: Under SOX, who must certify the accuracy of financial reports at a public company?
r: The chief executive and chief financial officers
Executives are personally responsible.
w: Customers do not certify the reports.

q: What is a whistleblower?
r: A person who reports illegal or unethical behavior
Laws protect them from retaliation.
w: A person who creates the company's budget
A person who audits tax returns

q: What does the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct require of CPAs?
r: Integrity, objectivity and due care
The code sets ethical standards for the profession.
w: Loyalty to the client above all
Some disclosure is required by law.

q: What does the principle of objectivity require of an accountant?
r: Being impartial and free of conflicts of interest
Judgments should not be influenced by bias.

q: What does confidentiality require of an accountant?
r: Not sharing client information without permission or legal duty
Clients trust accountants with sensitive data.

q: An accountant is offered a gift worth $500 by a client being audited. What is the best action?
r: Decline the gift to protect independence
Gifts can create the appearance of bias.
w: Accept it but give a better opinion
Accept it only if the client asks
The reason does not remove the conflict.

q: A manager asks an accountant to delay recording $15,000 of expenses so a loan application looks better. What should the accountant do?
r: Refuse and record the expenses in the proper period
Misstating results to deceive a lender is unethical and illegal.
w: Do it because the manager is in charge
Following orders does not excuse misreporting.

q: Which situation shows a conflict of interest?
r: An accountant prepares the books of a company owned by their spouse and approves their own work
Their independent judgment is in doubt.
w: An accountant meets a filing deadline

q: How long should businesses generally keep tax records?
r: At least three years, and longer in some cases
Many records must be kept for several years.
w: Records are not tied to sales.
Records are required for audits and filings.

q: What is a code of ethics?
r: A written set of values and standards for behavior
It guides decisions at work.

q: What is the purpose of the materiality concept?
r: Only items large enough to affect decisions need separate reporting
Tiny amounts can be treated simply.
w: All items must be reported separately
Revenue is reported at market value

q: A $20 stapler bought by a large company is expensed immediately instead of depreciated. Which concept supports this?
r: Materiality
The amount is too small to matter.

q: The conservatism principle says that when in doubt, an accountant should:
r: Choose the option that is less likely to overstate assets or income
It avoids misleading optimism.
w: Choose the option that raises income the most

q: What does the full disclosure principle require?
r: Reporting all information that could influence a user's decisions
Notes and statements together should be complete.

q: A lawsuit against a company is likely to cost $200,000. How should it be reported?
r: Recorded as a loss and disclosed
A probable and estimable loss must be recorded.
w: A lawsuit loss is not revenue.

q: What does IFRS stand for?
r: International Financial Reporting Standards
They are used in many countries outside the United States.
w: This is not a standards body.
This is not the correct name.

q: Why does the existence of IFRS and GAAP create a challenge for global companies?
r: Rules differ, making it harder to compare financial statements
Companies may need to convert between systems.
w: Both are identical in every respect
Neither can be used in any country
IFRS bans the use of inventory

q: Which tax form do most employers use to report wages paid to an employee at year end?
r: Form W-2
It reports wages and taxes withheld.
w: This tells the employer how much to withhold.

q: Which form reports payments of $600 or more to an independent contractor?
r: Form 1099-NEC
It reports nonemployee compensation.
w: This is an employer's quarterly tax return.

q: What does an employee complete so the employer knows how much tax to withhold?
r: Form W-4
It records filing status and allowances.
w: The employer issues this at year end.
This is the individual income tax return.

q: What is the purpose of Form I-9?
r: To verify an employee's identity and eligibility to work
Employers must keep it on file.
w: This is not a government form.

q: Which statement about independent auditors is true?
r: They must be independent of the company they audit
Independence supports a credible opinion.
w: They are employees who report to the managers whose work they audit
They guarantee the company has no fraud
Audits give reasonable, not absolute, assurance.
They prepare the company's daily entries
They examine records, not create them.

q: What is the difference between an internal and an external auditor?
r: Internal auditors work for the company; external auditors are independent firms
Their reports go to different users.
w: Internal auditors work for the IRS
External auditors work only for the company

q: What is the main goal of a financial audit?
r: To give an opinion on whether statements are fairly presented
It adds credibility to the numbers.

q: What does Generally Accepted Auditing Standards (GAAS) guide?
r: How auditors conduct their examinations
It sets quality expectations for auditors.

q: What does 'compliance' mean in accounting?
r: Following the laws, rules and standards that apply
It reduces legal and financial risk.

q: What can happen if a business fails to comply with tax laws?
r: Penalties, interest and possible legal action
Noncompliance can be costly.
w: Refunds are not triggered by noncompliance.
Audits can be an unwelcome result.

q: What does the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) prohibit?
r: Bribing foreign government officials to win business
It applies to U.S. companies abroad.

q: The Fair Labor Standards Act sets rules for which accounting-related area?
r: Minimum wage and overtime pay
Payroll records must follow it.

q: An employee is paid $15 per hour and works 46 hours in a week. Overtime is paid at 1.5 times after 40 hours. What is gross pay?
w: This pays all hours at the normal rate.
This pays all hours at the overtime rate.

q: What do FICA taxes fund?
r: Social Security and Medicare
Employees and employers both contribute.
w: This is funded by other taxes.
These are funded by state and local taxes.

q: An employee earns $2,000 gross. FICA is 7.65% for the employee. How much is withheld for FICA?
Who pays unemployment taxes (FUTA) in most cases?
r: The employer
The employee does not pay federal unemployment tax.

q: What is the difference between an employee and an independent contractor for payroll?
r: Employers withhold taxes from employees but not from contractors
Contractors handle their own taxes.

q: A company misclassifies an employee as a contractor to avoid payroll taxes. What is the most likely result?
r: Back taxes, penalties and possible legal action
Misclassification is a compliance violation.

q: What is data privacy in accounting?
r: Protecting sensitive financial and personal information
Records often contain private data.
w: Deleting all old data every day
Records must be kept as required.

q: Which practice best protects accounting data on a computer?
r: Strong passwords and regular backups
They guard against unauthorized access and loss.
w: Sharing one login among all staff
Keeping the only copy on a flash drive
One copy can easily be lost.

q: An accountant finds an error in a prior-year financial statement that is material. What is the proper action?
r: Correct it and disclose the correction
Material errors must be corrected and explained.
w: Leave it because the year is closed
